parts.partTitle: Why Heap Allocations Kill p99 Latency

beats.headline: Why does a 200-microsecond GC pause ruin your trade?
beats.subline: In high-frequency systems, even a tiny allocation burst skews p99.9 latency.
beats.narration: In high-frequency trading, a 200-microsecond GC pause is an eternity. If you want to hit microsecond targets, you stop tweaking GC flags and start starving the collector entirely.

beats.title: Standard vs. Zero-Alloc Path
beats.narration: Standard Java allocates objects per event, filling Eden and triggering pauses. Zero-allocation patterns pre-allocate pools at startup, keeping the steady-state loop completely garbage-free.

beats.title: Escape Analysis: The Compiler's Secret

steps.explanation: C2 proves the object never escapes, so it splits the fields into registers.

beats.narration: HotSpot's C2 compiler uses Escape Analysis to prove an object never leaves a method. If it succeeds, it performs scalar replacement, splitting the object into CPU registers.

beats.title: When Escape Analysis Fails

top.label: Optimized
top.code:
PriceWindow w = new PriceWindow(a, b);
return w.bid();

bottom.label: Heap Allocated
bottom.code:
PriceWindow w = new PriceWindow(a, b);
list.add(w); // Escapes!

beats.narration: Don't bet your SLA on it. If an object escapes to a list or a megamorphic method call, scalar replacement breaks and you're back to heap allocation.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
takeaways: Escape Analysis is a bonus, not a guarantee
Treat every 'new' in a hot loop as a bug

beats.headline: Stop creating DTOs for every incoming packet.
beats.subline: Mutable flyweights let you read raw buffers without copying data.
beats.narration: Stop creating DTOs for every incoming packet. Mutable flyweights let you read raw network buffers directly, avoiding object overhead entirely.

beats.title: The Flyweight Pattern

steps.explanation: One object instance reused for every incoming packet.

beats.narration: Instead of a new object per message, create one flyweight at startup. Call wrap on every packet to point it at the new buffer offset. Zero allocation, zero copying.

beats.title: Standard vs. Primitive Collections
beats.narration: Standard maps box primitives into objects, wasting 80 bytes per entry. Primitive collections like Agrona store data in flat arrays, eliminating boxing and pointer chasing.

beats.title: Agrona Primitive Map

steps.explanation: Avoid resizing during trading hours to keep latency flat.

beats.narration: Pre-size your primitive maps at startup. This prevents rehashing during your hot loop, ensuring consistent performance when it matters most.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: CPU Core Pinning and Thread Affinity →
beats.narration: Flyweights and primitive maps are your best friends. In Part 3, we pin threads to CPU cores to stop OS scheduling jitter.

beats.headline: Why is your Java thread jumping between CPU cores?
beats.subline: Cache misses and migration cost you precious microseconds.
beats.narration: Even without allocations, your thread can suffer jitter if the OS migrates it between cores. Cold caches will destroy your performance.

beats.title: Pinning Threads with Affinity

steps.explanation: Uses JNA to call sched_setaffinity on Linux.

beats.narration: Use OpenHFT's Affinity library to pin your worker thread to a specific physical core. This keeps your L1 and L2 caches warm and avoids NUMA cross-socket latency.

beats.title: Kernel-Level Isolation
beats.caption: Isolate cores from the Linux scheduler
beats.narration: Pinning isn't enough. You must isolate cores via kernel boot parameters so the OS scheduler doesn't place background tasks on your hot cores.

beats.title: Sources of Jitter
beats.narration: Context switches, cache migrations, and CPU power-saving states all introduce jitter. Isolation and pinning remove these variables.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
beats.narration: Pin your threads and isolate your cores. In Part 4, we finish by making logging garbage-free.

beats.headline: Your logger is secretly filling your heap.
beats.subline: Standard logging creates arrays and boxed objects for every single line.
beats.narration: Your logger is secretly filling your heap. Every log line creates boxed objects and arrays, triggering GC cycles when you least expect it.

beats.title: Garbage-Free Log4j2

steps.explanation: Formats primitives into reusable thread-local buffers.

beats.narration: Use Log4j2's garbage-free mode. The Unbox helper formats primitives into pre-allocated thread-local buffers, avoiding the heap entirely.

beats.title: Log4j2 JVM Flags
beats.caption: Enable async ring buffers
beats.narration: Set these flags to enable the async ring buffer and direct encoders. This ensures log events are processed without allocating temporary objects.

beats.title: Logging Performance
beats.narration: Standard logging creates a new LogEvent and object array for every call. Log4j2's async mode uses a pre-allocated ring buffer for total garbage-free operation.

beats.title: Zero-Allocation Mastery
